title: Lead enrichment: How it works and how to check data quality
summary: See how lead enrichment works, spot inaccurate data, and compare tools using a worked example and cost per usable record.
body_markdown:
Lead enrichment adds or updates details about a prospect, such as their current role, company size, or work email. Sales teams use this information to decide whether an account fits their market and how to approach the right person.


A rep preparing an email might find an old job title and no employee count in the lead record. Before writing the message, they need to establish who the person works for and whether the company is suitable.


B2B lead enrichment helps fill those gaps. However, returned information still needs review. An email can pass verification even though it belongs to someone at their previous employer.


## What is lead enrichment?


An enrichment service starts with information you already have, such as a name and company domain. It uses those identifiers to look for further details about the person or business.


Contact enrichment covers an individual’s professional details. Company enrichment adds information such as industry, location, and employee count. Both are part of B2B data enrichment.


For example,[HubSpot’s enrichment documentation](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/records/how-data-enrichment-works-in-hubspot) describes matching selected records against its dataset, third-party providers, and public information. When it finds verified business information, it updates supported fields.


The same software may handle several related tasks:


Process What it does


Lead generation Finds or attracts potential customers


Lead enrichment Adds or updates information about those prospects


Email verification Checks an address using the provider’s verification methods


Data cleaning Fixes issues such as duplicates and inconsistent formats


Lead scoring Applies rules or a model to prioritize prospects


Enrichment supplies information that scoring rules can use. For instance, the employee count describes the company; your rules determine whether that size makes it a priority.


## Which lead data should you enrich?


Decide what you need to know before choosing fields. A team selling to operations leaders at software companies may need current responsibilities and business type more than a long list of social profiles.


Field Decision it supports What to check


Current employer and role Whether this person is relevant Employment is current and responsibilities fit


Company domain and business type Whether the account fits your market Correct business, including parent or subsidiary


Employee count or size range Which segment or territory applies Date, estimate status, and scope


Work email or business phone How to contact the person Verification status and correct person-company match


Technology used Whether your product is compatible Evidence of current use


Dated company change Whether there is a timely reason to research further Source, event date, and relevance


Required fields will vary. Territory routing may depend on location, while a campaign about an integration may need evidence that the company uses a particular CRM.


Also, distinguish company news from evidence of a purchase decision. Hiring salespeople confirms recruitment. It tells you nothing by itself about a budget or a need for your product.


Our guide to[researching a B2B prospect before outreach](https://blog.floworks.ai/how-to-research-a-b2b-prospect-before-outreach/) explains how to turn account facts into a relevant opening question.


## How does lead enrichment work?


Your provider and systems determine how much you can automate, from matching a record to applying reviewed updates.


### 1. Match the correct person or company


Start with the strongest identifiers you have, such as a work email, company domain, or professional profile URL.


Names alone can leave room for error. Two people may share a name, and one business may have several brands or subsidiaries. If you cannot confirm the match, pause the update and review it.


### 2. Retrieve the fields you need


The service searches its available sources for the requested details. These may include business databases or public web pages.


Save the source and relevant dates when available. An appointment announcement may be several years old even if you found it today. The retrieval date tells you when you accessed the page, which can differ from when the information changed.


### 3. Resolve conflicting information


Compare new values with the information your team already holds. A rep may have confirmed a role during a recent call while an external source still shows an older title.


Set permissions before allowing automatic changes. Decide which fields the service may fill and which it may overwrite.[Apollo’s CRM enrichment setup](https://knowledge.apollo.io/hc/en-us/articles/4413921630989-Use-CRM-Enrichment) , for example, requires field mapping and auto-fill or overwrite permissions before a run.


### 4. Apply approved updates


After review, send accepted fields to the appropriate system. The tool may support a CSV import, a native integration, or an API.


Keep do-not-contact flags and other exclusions in place. Also, retain enough history to investigate a changed value. Include these controls when planning your[CRM automation workflow](https://blog.floworks.ai/crm-automation-in-sales/) .


### 5. Use the reviewed record


With the updated information, your team can segment accounts, route leads, or continue qualification. Reps can also prepare questions for outreach.


Apply your targeting rules at this stage. A record can be complete and still describe an account outside your market.


## Manual, automated, and waterfall enrichment


Manual research helps when a record needs judgment, such as resolving conflicting employment details. Automation can handle routine lookups across a larger list.


Batch enrichment processes a group of records together. Triggered enrichment starts after a defined event, such as a new lead entering a supported CRM workflow.


Waterfall enrichment queries providers in sequence, often trying another source when a field is missing. It can expand coverage, although the returned values still need matching and validation checks.


A small team can begin with a limited batch and review it manually. Once the results meet the team’s requirements, it can decide which steps to automate.


## A lead enrichment example: What should you trust?


The following example is fictional. All names, companies, and evidence are invented to illustrate the review.


A team sells account-research software to growing B2B software companies. Its CRM lists Maya Shah as a sales director at Cedar Software. An enrichment run returns these updates:


Returned information Evidence in this example Decision


Maya now leads sales at Harbor Systems A recent appointment announcement and a matching professional profile Accept the employment update after confirming identity


An email at Cedar Software passes verification The address belongs to her previous employer Reject it for outreach to Maya at Harbor


Harbor has 240 employees An undated provider estimate Review if company size determines eligibility


Harbor uses a particular CRM An old job advert mentions experience with that CRM Keep current usage unconfirmed


Harbor is hiring account executives A current vacancy on its careers page Accept the hiring fact; leave purchase intent unconfirmed


Maya’s current role has supporting evidence. Her old email, however, is unsuitable for contacting her at Harbor.


Before reaching out, the rep needs a current contact route and a reason the hiring activity might matter. One possible question is: “How are your new account executives choosing which accounts to prioritize?”


This gives Maya room to explain the situation. The vacancy alone does not establish that Harbor has an account-research problem.


## How to check lead enrichment quality before scaling


Choose a test sample that reflects the accounts you plan to contact. Include your target roles and regions, along with difficult records such as job changes or incomplete company names.


Define what must be true before a record is usable. For one campaign, you might require a confirmed current employer, a relevant role, and a suitable work email.


Then separate the following measures:


Measure What you count


Required-field completion Records with every required field populated


Checked field accuracy Returned values confirmed against suitable evidence


Usable-record yield Input records that pass all checks for the intended workflow


Keep unresolved values separate from confirmed information. If you cannot verify a field, leave its status unknown.


### Why completion can overstate usable output


Suppose you submit 50 records. This calculation is hypothetical and is not a vendor benchmark.


The results break down as follows:


- 40 records return every required field.
- Of those 40, review confirms that 30 pass all campaign checks.
- Six contain an incorrect required value.
- Four remain unresolved.
- The remaining 10 records lack at least one required field.


Required-field completion is 40 ÷ 50 × 100, or 80%.


Usable-record yield is 30 ÷ 50 × 100, or 60%.


If the run costs $120, the data cost per usable record is $120 ÷ 30, or $4. Add review labor and other relevant costs when comparing the full workflow.


In this example, 40 records came back complete, but only 30 were ready for the campaign. Reporting both results makes the unresolved work visible.


After launch, measure research time and qualified conversations separately. Reply rates also depend on targeting, messaging, and delivery, so they cannot establish enrichment accuracy on their own.


## How to choose a lead enrichment tool


A demonstration shows how a tool works. Testing your own records helps you judge whether it suits your market.


Ask each provider:


- Does it return the fields your workflow requires?
- How does it handle ambiguous person and company matches?
- Can you inspect sources, dates, and verification status?
- What does its “verified” label mean?
- Can you protect existing values and review conflicting updates?
- Does it support the export or integration your team needs today?
- What do failed lookups, repeat checks, and contact details cost?
- How does it handle submitted records and deletion requests?


Record the answers alongside your sample results. Compare cost per usable record and the manual work your team would still need to do.

## Frequently asked questions


### How often should you enrich lead records?


Base the schedule on how you use the data. Check important contact details before an active campaign. Review records when you discover a job change or conflicting information. A dormant account list may need a different schedule from incoming leads.


### What should happen when no match is found?


Leave the value missing and send the record for review if that information matters to the task. Try a stronger identifier or another source. Avoid guessing contact details to complete a row.


### Can a small sales team start without a CRM integration?


Yes. Start with a small list and define the fields you need. Review the results in a spreadsheet, keeping accepted updates separate from unresolved records. Once that process works, assess whether automation would save enough repeat work to justify the setup.


## Run a small enrichment test


Choose one task, such as preparing a target-account list for outreach. Define the required fields, test a sample, and record which results pass or need further review before updating the full list.
